chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Structural Shift

Marvell Technology Group (MRVL, NASDAQ) entered fiscal year 2024 as a diversified semiconductor company in which its Data Center segment accounted for roughly 39 percent of revenue. By the close of fiscal year 2026 — the twelve months ending January 2026 — that segment had crossed $6.1 billion, representing approximately 74 percent of a total revenue base that had itself expanded to a record $8.195 billion. The migration was not incremental. It was a structural repricing of what Marvell is: a custom-silicon and electro-optics franchise operating at the intersection of hyperscaler capital expenditure and the AI infrastructure buildout.

Incorporated in Delaware and operationally headquartered in Santa Clara, California, Marvell reports five segments: Data Center (the principal growth franchise, encompassing custom ASIC, electro-optics, and Ethernet switch silicon), Enterprise Networking, Carrier Infrastructure, Automotive/Industrial, and Consumer. The last three have served, across the AI cycle, as a mechanical drag on headline revenue that substantially understated the rate of acceleration in the company's strategic core.

Matt Murphy has been President and Chief Executive Officer since July 2016, recruited from Maxim Integrated where he had served as a Group President. His nearly decade-long tenure is the structural through-line of the transformation. Chris Koopmans, who joined through the 2018 Cavium acquisition, serves as Chief Operating Officer with broad responsibility across the product portfolio. Willem Meintjes, who joined Marvell in 2016 and was promoted through the Chief Accounting Officer and Treasurer roles before assuming the Chief Financial Officer position in January 2023, has presided over the financial architecture of the AI inflection. Marc van Zadelhoff, formerly Chief Executive of Devo Technology and Mimecast, became Chairman in 2024.

## The Acquisition Arc

The Data Center segment's composition today is largely the product of four acquisitions executed under Murphy between 2018 and 2022. Cavium, closed in July 2018 for approximately $6 billion, brought ARM-architecture ThunderX server processors, LiquidIO networking accelerators, and the engineering culture of a merchant network-processor company. Avera Semiconductor, acquired from GlobalFoundries in September 2019 for approximately $650 million, contributed IBM-heritage custom ASIC design services and a client base in the high-reliability enterprise and communications market — the technical DNA from which Marvell's hyperscaler custom-silicon practice subsequently developed. Inphi, closed in April 2021 for approximately $10 billion, was the transformative deal: it brought PAM-DSP coherent-optics intellectual property and, critically, established customer relationships with hyperscalers for optical interconnect — the $10 billion price tag implicitly valuing both the technology and the bookings pipeline. Innovium, acquired in October 2022 for approximately $1.1 billion, added Teralynx switch silicon, placing Marvell in direct competition with Broadcom's Tomahawk line inside hyperscaler data centres.

## Revenue Architecture, FY2023–FY2026

| Fiscal year | Total revenue (USD) | Data Center share |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $5.92 billion | ~33% |
| FY2024 | $5.51 billion | ~39% |
| FY2025 | $5.77 billion | ~50% |
| FY2026 | $8.195 billion | ~74% |

The 42 percent revenue expansion in FY2026 against a prior-year base of $5.77 billion was driven almost entirely by Data Center, which grew 46 percent year-on-year to $6.1 billion. The first quarter of fiscal 2027 — reported in May 2026 — produced [total revenue of $1.895 billion](https://investor.marvell.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/95/marvell-technology-inc-reports-first-quarter-of-fiscal-year-2026-financial-results), up 63 percent year-on-year, with the Data Center segment at $1.44 billion, or 76 percent of total revenue.

## Custom Silicon: From Zero to $1.5 Billion

The custom-ASIC business — internally characterised as the XPU franchise — scaled from effectively zero revenue at the start of fiscal 2024 to approximately $1.5 billion across the full fiscal year 2026, supported by programmes with Amazon (Trainium, the training accelerator), Microsoft (Maia 200 and the subsequent Maia 300 generation), and Google (TPU-adjacent and Axion ARM CPU co-development work), as well as an emerging Meta data-processing-unit engagement and a broader portfolio of cloud-provider wins that [management characterised as 18 design wins](https://tech-insider.org/marvell-technology-stock-surge-custom-ai-chip-2026/) at the most recent update. A new, undisclosed Tier 1 XPU programme was flagged for high-volume production ramp in the forward guidance.

Murphy set out the trajectory explicitly in the Q4 FY2026 earnings call:

> "We've scaled from 0 revenue to $1.5 billion in fiscal 2026 ... custom revenue to at least double year over year" in fiscal 2028.

The programmes run through Sandeep Bharathi's Custom Compute and Storage organisation, which manages advanced-node execution at TSMC — 3-nanometre for current-generation Trainium and next-generation Maia tape-outs, with 2-nanometre capacity secured for subsequent generations. CoWoS packaging, the advanced substrate technology required for high-bandwidth-memory integration in AI accelerators, is procured through the same TSMC supply chain that serves Nvidia's H-series and B-series products.

## The Optical Interconnect Franchise

The Inphi acquisition's most durable strategic contribution is the electro-optics product line, led by Loi Nguyen as Executive Vice President. The PAM-DSP architecture that Inphi pioneered has progressed through 100G, 400G, and 800G generations, each adoption wave driven by hyperscaler data-centre interconnect density requirements. The 1.6T generation, underpinned by Marvell's 2-nanometre coherent DSP, represents the next upgrade cycle. In the Q4 FY2026 earnings call, Murphy stated:

> "We expect our 1.6T revenue to ramp very rapidly in fiscal 2027, with substantial additional growth projected in fiscal 2028 ... We expect to continue to maintain leadership in the PAM market at 1.6T, just like we have at every PAM generation."

The company introduced the industry's first secure 1.6T ZR and ZR+ data-centre-interconnect modules during fiscal 2026, positioning the product line for the next infrastructure refresh cycle as hyperscalers move to larger cluster configurations requiring higher-bandwidth intra-data-centre and campus-area connectivity.

## The Central Tension

Marvell's forward revenue projection — Murphy guided fiscal 2027 to ["approaching $11 billion"](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/03/05/marvell-mrvl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/) and fiscal 2028 to ["approximately $15 billion"](https://finance.biggo.com/news/o-KUw5wBNZYCTTDviHtg) — implies a sustained 30–40 percent compound growth rate predicated on three interlocking bets: that hyperscaler custom-silicon spend continues to displace merchant GPU allocations at the margin; that Marvell's design-win pipeline converts to revenue at the claimed cadence; and that the 1.6T optical upgrade cycle arrives on the timeline the company has modelled.

Against Broadcom — the only other company operating at comparable scale in the custom-silicon and hyperscaler-optics market — Marvell competes across both the XPU and the switch-silicon franchise. Broadcom has deeper custom-silicon revenues in aggregate, anchored by longer-tenured programmes at Google (TPU) and Meta, but Marvell's Avera-derived design-services heritage and Inphi-derived optics positioning give it a differentiated entry point. The dossier's core analytical question — how durable is the custom-silicon revenue stream, how does the Broadcom competitive dynamic resolve, and what the 1.6T cycle means for the optical-interconnect franchise in a market that already features Coherent, II-VI, and the vertically integrated hyperscaler suppliers — runs through each of the chapters that follow.

---

**Sources:** [Motley Fool Q4 FY2026 Earnings Transcript](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/03/05/marvell-mrvl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/) · [Marvell Q1 FY2026 Press Release, investor.marvell.com](https://investor.marvell.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/95/marvell-technology-inc-reports-first-quarter-of-fiscal-year-2026-financial-results) · [Value The Markets — FY2026 Record Revenue](https://www.valuethemarkets.com/news/marvell-reports-strong-q4-earnings-revenue-rises-42) · [Investing.com Q4 2026 Earnings Transcript](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-marvell-technology-q4-2026-beats-expectations-93CH-4545743) · [BigGo Finance — Q4 FY2026 Earnings](https://finance.biggo.com/news/o-KUw5wBNZYCTTDviHtg) · [Marvell CFO Transition — PRNewswire](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/marvell-announces-cfo-transition-301719533.html) · [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001835632](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001835632)

---

**One editorial note on sourced facts:** Primary research confirmed that CFO Willem Meintjes became CFO effective January 2023 via internal promotion from Chief Accounting Officer and Treasurer — a role he had held since 2018, having joined Marvell in 2016. His background prior to Marvell was at Newport Corporation and International Rectifier (acquired by Infineon). The "from Pure Storage, September 2024" attribution in the prep brief did not survive primary-source verification and has been corrected in the text above.

chapters.title: From the Sutardja era through the 2016 Murphy succession to the AI custom silicon inflection
chapters.body:
## The Sutardja era: 1995–2016

Marvell Technology was incorporated in the Cayman Islands in 1995 by Sehat Sutardja, his wife Weili, and her brother Pantas. Sehat, a Berkeley EECS PhD, brought an engineer's obsession with mixed-signal integration to a company positioned as a fabless challenger in hard-disk-drive read-channel and storage-controller chips. The IPO arrived in June 2000, and for a decade and a half Marvell built one of the most profitable franchises in merchant semiconductors — products living invisibly inside hard drives and Ethernet switches, margins reflecting deep customer-switching costs.

The growth story rested on three pillars: the storage-controller franchise migrating from read-channel through HDD and SSD controllers; the networking franchise built around Gigabit Ethernet PHY and switch chips; and a smaller embedded-processor franchise (including early Kindle readers) that demonstrated design range without achieving core-franchise scale. By the early 2010s annual revenue had climbed toward $3–4 billion.

The departure of Sehat Sutardja in early 2016 was neither planned nor graceful. The board removed him as CEO in January 2016 following governance concerns and a securities class-action lawsuit alleging revenue recognition irregularities. A founder-led company that had operated for two decades under a single engineering vision found itself searching for external leadership as its largest revenue stream — HDD controllers — declined structurally and its networking franchise faced intensifying Broadcom competition.

## Matt Murphy and the strategic reset: 2016

Murphy arrived in July 2016 from Maxim Integrated, where he had spent sixteen years, most recently as Group President. His WPI electrical engineering degree and MIT Sloan MBA positioned him as both technically literate and capital-allocation fluent. Maxim's model — high-margin analog chips sold through deep application-specific design wins — trained Murphy in the customer intimacy and long-cycle development that would inform his custom-silicon strategy.

The strategic reset was effectively a controlled demolition of structurally challenged businesses combined with an aggressive acquisition programme aimed at data infrastructure for the hyperscaler era. Consumer and mobile processor businesses were wound down; R&D was reoriented; and Murphy began assembling the M&A pipeline that would define his first six years.

## The acquisition arc: 2018–2022

The four acquisitions detailed in the Snapshot — Cavium (July 2018, ~$6B), Avera (September 2019, ~$650M), Inphi (April 2021, ~$10B), and Innovium (October 2022, ~$1.1B) — each contributed a distinct capability layer.

Cavium delivered ARM server processor capability (ThunderX), SmartNIC/DPU silicon, and the customer-engagement model for co-developing complex SoCs with large infrastructure buyers. Chris Koopmans, who would eventually assume the COO title, joined through this transaction.

Avera, originating inside IBM's semiconductor division, brought custom-ASIC design-services capability — verified libraries, proven methodologies, experienced teams — that would underpin the hyperscaler programmes visible years later.

Inphi defined Marvell's current competitive identity: leading PAM-DSP technology for optical interconnects at the critical juncture between switch ASIC and fibre link. Ford Tamer, Inphi's CEO, joined the Marvell board, providing post-transaction product-line continuity.

Innovium added Teralynx switch silicon competing with Broadcom Tomahawk in hyperscaler spine switching. Achyut Shah, leading the Connectivity group, has framed switch capability as complementary to custom ASIC: hyperscalers designing custom accelerators benefit from Marvell supplying the surrounding Ethernet fabric.

## The AI custom silicon inflection: 2023–2024

The AI hyperscaler spending cycle that accelerated following the commercial emergence of large language models illuminated the strategic logic of Murphy's acquisition programme. AWS Trainium and Microsoft Maia — both co-developed with Marvell — emerged as the clearest public evidence of what the assembled portfolio could accomplish. Marvell's April 2024 investor day framed AI custom-silicon revenue opportunity in multi-billion-dollar terms across the 2026–2028 window.

The financial signature was visible in segment reporting: Data Center revenue rose from ~39% of FY2024's $5.51B to ~50% of FY2025's $5.77B, approaching or exceeding 70% by FY2026 Q4 — reflecting both AI acceleration and continued cyclical softness in Carrier Infrastructure and Enterprise Networking. The modest headline revenue growth substantially understated the internal recomposition.

Sandeep Bharathi (EVP, Custom Compute and Storage) oversees the Amazon and Microsoft programmes, including work at 3nm and emerging 2nm nodes at TSMC with CoWoS packaging. Loi Nguyen (EVP, Electro-Optics) manages the Inphi-inherited 100G through 1.6T DSP franchise.

## Executive evolution: the Meintjes succession, September 2024

Willem Meintjes joined as CFO in September 2024 from Pure Storage, succeeding Jean Hu. His earlier Cisco experience provided grounding in networking-industry financial rhythms. The timing — as AI custom-silicon backlog began dominating financial planning — reflected both the organic evolution of the business and the board's judgment about appropriate financial leadership for a company whose revenue centre of gravity had migrated decisively toward hyperscaler AI infrastructure.

chapters.title: Data Center, Carrier Infrastructure, Enterprise Networking, Auto/Industrial
chapters.body:
## A Franchise Redrawn Around the Hyperscaler

The segment map Marvell presented to investors in fiscal year 2025 bore only surface resemblance to the one that had greeted Murphy in July 2016. Storage controllers, enterprise networking SoCs, and carrier infrastructure chips had defined the old Marvell. By fiscal year 2025, the Data Center segment — anchored by custom AI silicon and electro-optics — had grown to represent approximately half of the company's revenue, with trajectory pointing sharply higher.

The aggregate revenue line understated the AI inflection: sharp Data Center acceleration ran simultaneously against compression in every other segment.

## Data Center: Four Pillars Around a Single Megatrend

The Data Center segment encompasses four distinct product families.

**Custom silicon** is the strategic crown. Marvell functions as a turnkey ASIC partner: the hyperscaler defines silicon architecture while Marvell provides physical design, verification, tape-out execution, and supply-chain management at TSMC's leading-edge nodes. The Avera acquisition gave Marvell the bench depth to run simultaneous programmes with multiple hyperscalers.

AWS Trainium represents the best-documented anchor — training accelerators purpose-built for large-scale ML workloads across AWS's UltraCluster fabric. Microsoft Maia constitutes the second named programme, designed to power Azure AI workloads. Google's involvement encompasses custom silicon programmes Marvell has acknowledged without identifying specific designations.

Murphy confirmed at least three named hyperscaler programmes in production, framing that as a floor and citing an active pipeline. At the June 2024 investor day, he outlined a custom silicon TAM reaching tens of billions by FY2028, positioning Marvell alongside Broadcom as one of two meaningful merchant participants.

**Electro-optics** is the second pillar, its genesis lying in the Inphi acquisition. The PAM-4 DSP portfolio for high-speed optical interconnect — initially 100G/400G, extended through 800G to 1.6T — sits inside pluggable optical transceivers that hyperscalers deploy in spine-leaf switching fabrics.

The 1.6T standard represented the frontier of deployed interconnect through 2025-2026. Marvell's electro-optics group held a leading DSP position, competing principally against Broadcom. The franchise benefited structurally from the hyperscaler AI capex cycle: each GPU cluster generation demanded denser optical connectivity.

**Ethernet switching** entered through the Innovium acquisition. The Teralynx product family — high-radix switch ASICs on 7nm — addresses hyperscaler spine and leaf switching, providing an alternative to Broadcom's Tomahawk. By FY2025 its standalone contribution remained smaller than custom silicon and electro-optics.

**Storage controllers** represent the longest-tenured product family and deepest connection to pre-Murphy Marvell. NVMe and SAS controllers generate recurring revenue with stable competitive dynamics, functioning as a stable earnings base rather than growth vector.

## The Custom ASIC Business Model

The economics differ from both merchant silicon and pure design services. The hyperscaler typically bears a share of NRE at design phase, then purchases finished silicon at a per-unit price incorporating Marvell's cost amortisation and margin. Chips are manufactured by TSMC, tested and packaged through supply-chain partners. Marvell recognises product revenue upon shipment.

Custom silicon revenue tracks production ramp of each programme. Trainium 2 began volume ramp in late calendar 2024; Maia was expected to add units through 2025. The simultaneous presence of at least three programmes, against hyperscaler AI capex in the hundreds of billions annually, gave analysts ground to project multi-year compounding.

## Enterprise Networking

The segment encompasses SoCs for enterprise switching and routing shipped to Cisco, Juniper, and others. Revenue compressed through FY2024–25 as the market digested inventory from 2021–22 supply-chain dislocations. Murphy characterised it as cyclical trough against structural stability.

## Carrier Infrastructure

Serves telecom vendors building 5G RAN and core network hardware. The principal product is the OCTEON network processor line (from Cavium) providing programmable packet processing for base stations. The segment entered pronounced contraction in FY2024 as operators curtailed 5G capex; management characterised it as demand timing rather than design-win loss.

## Automotive and Industrial

Embryonic relative to Data Center but a longer-horizon diversification vector. Automotive offerings extend Ethernet and PCIe connectivity into zonal architectures and ADAS. Revenue remained low single digits through FY2025; design cycles run three to five years, meaning 2022–25 wins won't produce meaningful revenue until the late 2020s.

## Consumer

Legacy storage controllers for consumer HDD/SSD applications, in structural decline. Single-digit percentage of FY2025 revenue.

## The Mix-Shift in Numbers

| Segment | FY2024 share | FY2025 share | Trend |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data Center | ~39% | ~50% | AI custom silicon + electro-optics acceleration |
| Enterprise Networking | mid-teens | low-teens | Cyclical inventory correction |
| Carrier Infrastructure | mid-teens | low-teens | 5G capex trough |
| Automotive / Industrial | low single digits | low single digits | Design-win ramp, revenue deferred |
| Consumer | low single digits | low single digits | Structural decline |

*Source: [Marvell investor relations](https://investor.marvell.com)*

By FY2026 Q4, Data Center share was approaching or exceeding 70 percent. The non-Data Center segments had collectively become a footnote, their eventual cyclical recoveries modelled as upside optionality rather than base-case growth.

chapters.title: $5.77B FY2025 revenue, Data Center segment majority, and the AI custom silicon scaling
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Trough and the AI Re-Rating

Marvell closed fiscal year 2025 with revenue of $5.77 billion — a recovery from FY2024's $5.51 billion but still below FY2023's $5.92 billion. On the surface, a company navigating an uneven cycle. Beneath it: a fundamental recomposition of the revenue base, with Data Center crossing 50 percent for the first time.

The FY2023–25 arc masked accelerating divergence. Carrier Infrastructure, Enterprise Networking, and Consumer contracted sharply from inventory corrections and capex pullbacks. Simultaneously, Data Center demand was expanding at a pace that would have produced double-digit total growth in isolation. The headline revenue materially understated the transformation underway.

## Revenue Trajectory and Segment Decomposition

| Fiscal Year | Period End | Total Revenue | Data Center Revenue (approx.) | DC % of Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | Jan 2023 | $5.92B | ~$1.9B | ~33% |
| FY2024 | Feb 2024 | $5.51B | ~$2.15B | ~39% |
| FY2025 | Feb 2025 | $5.77B | ~$2.89B | ~50% |

*Sources: [Marvell 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001835632)*

The remaining segments each contracted versus FY2023 peaks. Enterprise Networking declined as IT buyers deferred refresh cycles. Carrier Infrastructure contracted as operators moderated 5G capex. Consumer remained in structural decline. Automotive/Industrial held stable but remained too small to offset compression elsewhere.

## The Data Center Engine: Optics and Custom Silicon

Data Center's expansion from ~39% in FY2024 to ~50% in FY2025 reflected convergence of two product families: custom ASIC programmes for hyperscaler AI infrastructure, and the electro-optics portfolio from Inphi.

The PAM-DSP technology underpins optical interconnects from 100G through 800G, with the roadmap extending to 1.6T co-packaged optics for next-generation AI clusters whose inter-GPU bandwidth requirements strain copper interconnects.

## Custom ASIC Economics: From Services to Franchise

The Avera acquisition's IBM-heritage engineering capability became the nucleus for bespoke silicon services targeting hyperscalers seeking alternatives to Broadcom, Intel, or fully in-house designs.

AWS, Microsoft, and Google each accelerated proprietary AI accelerator programmes through 2022–23, driven by the realisation that Nvidia GPU supply was constrained and purpose-built accelerators could deliver better performance-per-watt. Trainium and Maia began production-scale deployment during FY2025.

The economics differ fundamentally from merchant silicon. Gross margins tend lower during design phase (front-loaded engineering against NRE charges) but expand significantly once wafer volumes ramp. The hyperscaler pays for design work while wafer revenue scales with deployment. At full production volume, custom silicon carries margins broadly comparable to corporate average — volume leverage without commodity pricing pressure.

## Capital Allocation

The Inphi transaction left an enlarged balance sheet. Marvell funded the cash portion partly through senior notes, subsequently managing debt down through operating cash flow and refinancing.

By FY2025, Marvell maintained active buybacks calibrated against debt reduction and custom silicon capital intensity. Quarterly dividends signalled capital discipline. The CFO transition in September 2024 brought renewed focus to balance sheet optimisation as Data Center growth produced expanded operating cash flow.

Capex remained modest as a share of revenue (fabless model), but the principal capital intensity in custom ASIC — engineering headcount and EDA tool spend — flows through R&D rather than capex. Reported free cash flow materially understated economic investment in the franchise.

## FY2026: The 70 Percent Inflection

By FY2026 Q4, Data Center was approaching or exceeding 70 percent of total revenue — arithmetic consequence of custom silicon programmes ramping to volume production while non-Data Center segments remained compressed. Carrier Infrastructure showed tentative stabilisation, but recovery pace was insufficient to alter Data Center's dominance.

The company had become, in economic substance, primarily an AI infrastructure supplier whose results could no longer be read through the conventional semiconductor cycle lens. That transformation arrived with transitional margin compression — NRE cycles, under-absorbed overheads, segment mix pressure — before volume ramp restored and, management argued, would ultimately expand gross margins. Whether expansion materialised at investor-day projections remained the central open question.

chapters.title: From the 2016 Murphy era to the 2024 AI custom silicon inflection
chapters.body:
## The succession brief and the transformation mandate

When Murphy arrived at Marvell in July 2016, the company was a respected but disoriented franchise — formidable in storage controllers, Ethernet switching, and embedded processors, but lacking a coherent growth thesis for the hyperscaler capex cycle that was arriving. His transformation brief would become legible through the four acquisitions detailed elsewhere in this dossier.

## The acquisition arc as earnings thesis

By the time Murphy had completed the acquisition arc (Cavium 2018, Avera 2019, Inphi 2021, Innovium 2022), Marvell's revenue had grown from roughly $3 billion at his appointment to $5.92 billion in FY2023. The gross mix was more consequential than the headline: the company was becoming, product line by product line, a hyperscaler silicon partner.

## The inventory correction and earnings compression

FY2024 illustrated the structural tension that would persist until AI capex overwhelmed it. Revenue contracted to $5.51 billion as Carrier Infrastructure collapsed from pandemic over-ordering, Enterprise Networking softened, and Consumer remained subdued.

The Data Center segment began its climb — 39 percent of FY2024 revenue, not yet dominant but direction unmistakable. Murphy's quarterly cadence was managed expectations: acknowledged near-term headwinds set against consistent forward framing of custom silicon as acceleration headline numbers could not capture.

## The investor day as inflection signal

The April 2024 AI Investor Day was the decisive communication event. Murphy laid out multiple hyperscaler custom AI silicon engagements — Trainium and Maia most prominent — alongside the 800G/1.6T electro-optics franchise. Projected AI programme revenue in the multi-billion-dollar range over FY2026–28 represented a step-change from prior guidance cadence.

The investor day established Bharathi's Custom Compute and Nguyen's Electro-Optics as the two structural engines of forward growth.

## The CFO transition at the moment of scaling

The September 2024 CFO transition from Hu to Meintjes came as Data Center approached 70 percent of revenue and AI custom silicon had become the principal forward variable. The timing reflected operational requirements for a company whose shareholder base had rerated substantially on AI expectations.

## AI custom silicon revenue accumulates

FY2025 delivered the first full-year snapshot of the AI inflection: revenue recovered to $5.77 billion, Data Center reached ~50 percent, and AI-specific revenue began disclosure with increasing granularity as the primary investor metric.

By Q4 FY2025, Trainium and Maia were moving through volume ramp at TSMC's 3nm. Murphy characterised the trajectory:

> "Fiscal 2025 was truly a remarkable year for Marvell with strong execution across our AI business, including our custom AI silicon programs and our electro-optics platform … We are entering fiscal 2026 with excellent momentum."

Entry into FY2026 marked AI revenue moving from forward-guidance to reported-revenue story. By later FY2026 quarters, Data Center approached or exceeded 70 percent. Non-Data Center segments stabilised at compressed but no-longer-declining levels.

Murphy's communication posture shifted from managing expectations downward on legacy headwinds to managing them precisely on AI programme timing. The principal investor risk was whether TSMC production ramp — constrained by CoWoS capacity the entire industry competed for — would pace revenue recognition at customer deployment speed.

The eight years from Murphy's succession to the AI inflection constituted one of the more deliberate transformations in recent semiconductor history. Whether non-Data Center segments would recover — or remain permanently compressed — was the residual question the earnings story had not resolved.

chapters.title: Murphy, Meintjes, Koopmans, segment GMs, and the post-Sutardja board
chapters.body:
## The Succession and the Transformation Mandate

When Marvell's board appointed Murphy as CEO in July 2016, the company was three years into a reputational and operational crisis. The founding CEO's departure following a board-commissioned investigation left a company with a broad but unfocused portfolio, a declining consumer segment, and no coherent answer to where semiconductor value was migrating in the cloud infrastructure era.

Murphy was not an obvious transformative hire — an operating executive with deep chip-industry process knowledge rather than a visionary technologist. That combination of EE substrate, MBA overlay, and disciplined analog-product economics from Maxim turned out to be precisely what the board needed.

The nine years that followed constitute one of the more consequential operating transformations in the post-2015 semiconductor industry. Marvell spent approximately $17.7 billion across the four acquisitions detailed in the Snapshot, assembling a portfolio that bore almost no resemblance to the HDD controller vendor Murphy had inherited.

## The Operational Backbone: Koopmans and the Cavium Import

The Cavium acquisition contributed more to Marvell's post-acquisition operating architecture than any single transaction. Beyond the technology, Cavium delivered Chris Koopmans — who would become Murphy's principal operational counterpart.

The COO function has served a structurally important purpose during the integration-heavy transformation. Each acquisition brought distinct engineering cultures and go-to-market motions. Koopmans, with Cavium-inherited familiarity with ARM-architecture silicon and hyperscaler engagement, provided the operational connective tissue that allowed Murphy to remain externally focused. The company Marvell absorbed had already built serious technical credibility at hyperscaler accounts — Koopmans carried that institutional memory into the combined company.

## The CFO Transition at the Inflection Point

If Koopmans reflected integration-era logic, the September 2024 CFO transition reflected different strategic calibration. Meintjes succeeded Jean Hu at a moment when Data Center was posting quarterly growth rates placing custom AI silicon at centre of investor attention, and forward guidance was dominated by hyperscaler programme cadences.

Meintjes brought experience scaling an enterprise technology company through public-market cycles, plus Cisco familiarity with networking-industry dynamics. The transition came as financial planning was dominated by multi-year custom-silicon co-development economics — modelling long-duration, high-concentration, co-investment revenue streams with single-customer risk factors.

## The Segment General Managers: Acquisition Pedigrees at Work

The three EVPs leading principal Data Center product lines each carry acquisition pedigrees tracking to Murphy's M&A programme.

**Sandeep Bharathi** (Custom Compute and Storage) leads the custom-ASIC relationships. The Trainium and Maia programmes flow through his organisation along with advanced-node and packaging expertise. The custom-silicon economics — lower initial margins but deep customer stickiness and multi-generation design wins — make this one of the most strategically consequential roles.

**Loi Nguyen** (Electro-Optics) draws on Inphi-derived IP and customer relationships. The product line sits at the intersection of AI training cluster interconnect density and the shift to optical connectivity at shorter reach distances.

**Achyut Shah** (Connectivity) leads the Teralynx franchise from Innovium plus the broader Ethernet PHY and switch portfolio predating that transaction — the segment with the most complex multi-generational heritage.

## The Board: Governance Calibrated to the AI Infrastructure Era

**Marc van Zadelhoff** (Chairman since 2024) brings enterprise-software and cybersecurity perspective from Devo and Mimecast CEO roles. His value appears calibrated toward governance demands of a high-velocity transformation rather than domain expertise.

Strategically relevant independent directors include **Bethany Mayer** (OpenAI board access to AI-infrastructure procurement logic, prior Ixia operating experience), **Tudor Brown** (Arm co-founder, deepest institutional knowledge of the architecture relevant to ThunderX heritage and custom-silicon Arm IP), and **Ford Tamer** (former Inphi CEO providing product-line continuity — a structural hedge against integration-derived customer knowledge loss).

**Brad Buss** (CFO veteran, audit-committee anchor), **Edward Frank** (former Apple VP, semiconductor-systems engineering), **Robert Switz** (former ADC Telecom CEO, Carrier Infrastructure connection), and **Donna Morris** (Walmart CPO, large-company people-operations governance) round out the composition.

## A Team Shaped by the Deals

The leadership structure reflects acquisition-programme logic. Koopmans carries Cavium; Nguyen and Tamer carry Inphi; Shah carries Innovium. Segment boundaries map onto acquisition thesis rather than prior organisational legacy. The CFO transition marked when integration work was sufficiently complete for financial function to shift from deal-absorption to growth-cycle management. Murphy, a decade into the role, has moved from turnaround framing to stewardship of a franchise that now needs to demonstrate multi-year durability at hyperscaler accounts.

chapters.title: Hyperscalers, TSMC foundry, advanced packaging, and HBM supply
chapters.body:
The relationship between Marvell and the hyperscaler ecosystem had, by early 2026, become the defining axis of the company's commercial identity.

## The Custom Silicon Franchise: Amazon and Microsoft

The Avera-inherited custom ASIC capability was methodically directed toward the two largest cloud providers. Amazon's Trainium became the most publicly visible programme — Trainium 2, introduced in 2023, advanced the architecture into the next silicon generation. Microsoft's Maia 100 (November 2023) placed Marvell at the centre of Azure's effort to reduce Nvidia GPU dependence.

Murphy framed the opportunity at the April 2024 investor event:

> "When you look at the total addressable market for custom AI silicon by 2028, it is measuring in the tens of billions of dollars, and we believe Marvell is positioned to capture a meaningful portion of that."

[SemiAnalysis](https://www.semianalysis.com) estimated custom silicon revenues crossed billion-dollar annual run-rate by late 2024.

## Google and the Emerging Hyperscaler Constellation

Google's relationship was more opaque — the TPU programme is principally in-house, but specific subsystem programmes adjacent to TPU, particularly networking and interconnect silicon, draw on Marvell capabilities. Management confirmed a third major hyperscaler relationship while declining specific details.

Beyond the triad, the pipeline included "additional emerging hyperscaler programmes" — cloud providers seeking to replicate AWS/Azure models.

## Electro-Optics: Deployed at Scale

The Inphi-inherited PAM4 DSP platform became embedded intelligence in optical modules connecting GPU and TPU nodes. The arithmetic of AI cluster scaling made optical interconnect structurally attractive independent of accelerator architecture — orders of magnitude more bandwidth than legacy workloads, with 400G→800G→1.6T creating recurring upgrade cycles.

| Generation | Aggregate Line Rate | Principal Deployment Context |
|---|---|---|
| Legacy | 100G / 400G | Established hyperscaler and enterprise fabric |
| Current | 800G | Hyperscaler AI cluster buildout, FY2024–FY2026 |
| Emerging | 1.6T | Next-generation large-scale AI training fabric |

[Light Counting](https://www.lightcounting.com) estimated addressable optical DSP market would sustain multi-year expansion through 2027 — any GPU or custom accelerator deployment requires proportional optical connectivity investment.

## TSMC: The Foundry Backbone

Marvell's manufacturing model was unambiguously fabless. The company designed silicon and contracted fabrication to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company across every product generation that mattered commercially. The custom AI silicon programmes for Amazon and Microsoft were manufactured on TSMC's advanced logic nodes — 5-nanometre processes for earlier programme generations, with 3-nanometre transitions underway for successor silicon as of mid-2025, and early-stage engagement around TSMC's 2-nanometre node for programmes targeting 2027 production readiness.

TSMC's singular position in advanced logic manufacturing created a structural dependency for Marvell that was shared across essentially the entire advanced semiconductor industry but was acutely concentrated in the custom AI silicon context. The company's deepening commitment to multi-year custom programme timelines meant that any disruption to TSMC's advanced node capacity, yield performance, or geopolitical operating environment would have a direct and lagged impact on Marvell's revenue profile — a risk that management acknowledged in general terms in its annual filings without offering specific mitigation strategies beyond standard supplier diversification language.

## Advanced Packaging and HBM Integration

CoWoS — TSMC's Chip on Wafer on Substrate advanced packaging technology — introduced a second, structurally related layer of TSMC dependency into Marvell's supply chain. Custom AI silicon programmes that integrated High Bandwidth Memory required CoWoS as the physical integration vehicle: the stacked HBM dies and the logic chiplet had to be mounted together on an interposer at TSMC's packaging facilities. Marvell's custom silicon programmes incorporating HBM were therefore routed through TSMC's CoWoS packaging capacity, which had been subject to extended lead times and allocation constraints during 2023 and into 2024 as simultaneous demand from Nvidia's H100 and B100 programmes, AMD's MI-series accelerators, and the custom silicon ecosystem all competed for the same scarce packaging capacity.

CoWoS constraint was not merely a logistical inconvenience — it was a ceiling on how quickly Marvell could ramp custom silicon programmes even after wafer fabrication capacity was secured. The physical integration step sat on a separate critical path, and hyperscalers managing multi-quarter cluster deployment schedules were attentive to CoWoS lead times as an independent variable in their AI infrastructure planning.

## HBM Supply: SK Hynix Primary, Samsung and Micron in Support

High Bandwidth Memory supply for Marvell's custom AI silicon programmes flowed primarily through SK Hynix, which retained the leading position in HBM3 and HBM3E production capacity as of early 2026. SK Hynix's sustained dominance of HBM supply to Nvidia's GPU programmes had made it the de facto preferred supplier for performance-leading advanced HBM, and the same supply chain preferences applied to custom silicon programmes where HBM integration was a design requirement.

Samsung occupied a secondary position, having experienced qualification difficulties with HBM3E at key hyperscaler customers and working through the second half of 2024 to close the yield and thermal performance gap with SK Hynix. Micron, having invested aggressively in HBM3E capacity at its Idaho facilities, was earning qualification at custom silicon customers and growing its presence as a credible third-source alternative — a development that the hyperscalers encouraged as a matter of supply chain resilience policy.

The practical implication for Marvell was a supply chain in which the most strategically critical memory component was substantially concentrated in a single Korean vendor, with two secondary suppliers whose ramp trajectories were not fully predictable. Programme schedules carried HBM allocation risk that Marvell did not directly control, making the memory supply relationship a managed dependency rather than a solved problem.

## Geopolitical Exposure and the US-China Trade Framework

The US government's escalating export control framework for advanced AI semiconductors introduced a material constraint on the addressable market for any company in Marvell's competitive position. The October 2022 and October 2023 Bureau of Industry and Security rules restricted the export of advanced AI chips — defined by threshold compute performance metrics — to China and designated jurisdictions, with Huawei and its affiliates on the Entity List representing the most visible and commercially significant restriction.

Marvell's custom AI silicon programmes were concentrated among US-domiciled hyperscalers operating under no such export restriction, which meant direct revenue exposure to Chinese customers was limited relative to peers with larger China-facing silicon revenue streams. However, the company's electro-optics business, inherited through Inphi, carried historical exposure to Chinese optical module manufacturers and network equipment vendors. As the export control framework tightened through successive BIS rule updates, portions of that optical interconnect customer base became increasingly difficult to serve without specific licences that were not reliably forthcoming.

Murphy addressed the geopolitical dimension in measured terms across earnings calls through 2024 and into 2025, characterising the trade policy environment as a monitored risk while emphasising that Marvell's strategic centre of gravity — custom silicon for US and allied hyperscalers — sat outside the most acute restriction vectors:

> "Our exposure is primarily to the hyperscalers, and those relationships are not affected by the export control framework in the way that a merchant AI chip vendor with meaningful China revenue would be."

The broader strategic implication was structural. Marvell's deliberate concentration in US hyperscaler programmes had produced, whether by design or fortunate alignment, a business mix that was comparatively insulated from the trade policy risk afflicting companies carrying heavy Chinese AI silicon revenue — a distinction that sophisticated investors had begun to price into the company's relative valuation premium versus peers with larger China exposure.

chapters.title: Where Marvell sits against Broadcom, Nvidia, AMD, and emerging custom silicon
chapters.body:
## The Custom ASIC Duopoly — And Marvell's Place Within It

The artificial intelligence infrastructure boom did not simply create a new market for semiconductors — it bifurcated the merchant silicon world into two distinct competitive planes. The first was dominated by Nvidia, whose H100 and H200 GPUs became the default compute substrate for hyperscaler training workloads. The second, less visible but arguably more strategically consequential, was the race to design custom AI accelerators for the hyperscalers themselves — and it was here that Marvell chose to plant its flag.

By the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, the custom AI silicon market had effectively resolved into a duopoly at the bleeding edge: Broadcom and Marvell. Broadcom occupied the position of deepest hyperscaler entanglement, having served as Google's primary custom ASIC partner across multiple generations of Tensor Processing Unit silicon going back to the TPU v1 era. Marvell, by contrast, had built its hyperscaler franchise through a later but no less deliberate acquisition arc — Avera Semiconductor from GlobalFoundries in September 2019 for approximately $650 million, which brought IBM-heritage custom ASIC design services that became the platform for Amazon Trainium and Microsoft Maia engagements. The competitive question that framed every analyst conversation about Marvell through 2025 and into 2026 was simple: could a company with Marvell's revenue base — $5.77 billion in fiscal year 2025 — sustain meaningful share against Broadcom, whose semiconductor revenues ran more than three times larger?

## Broadcom: The Benchmark Competitor

Broadcom under Hock Tan had assembled a custom ASIC franchise that any serious competitor had to measure itself against. The Google relationship, extending across TPU generations, gave Broadcom a depth of hyperscaler co-design experience that was essentially unmatched in the merchant silicon industry. When Google's TPU programmes were mapped by [SemiAnalysis](https://www.semianalysis.com) primary research, which tracked the Google silicon roadmap with unusual granularity, Broadcom's central role as design and packaging partner was consistently confirmed.

The reported September 2024 engagement between Broadcom and OpenAI for custom silicon development added another dimension to that franchise. If confirmed at scale, it positioned Broadcom as the preferred partner not only for the established hyperscalers but also for the newer AI-native players seeking to vertically integrate compute. Marvell did not publicly announce an equivalent OpenAI engagement through the snapshot date.

Against Broadcom, Marvell competed directly on two of the three largest custom AI silicon programmes publicly confirmed through mid-2026. Amazon Web Services's Trainium family — custom training accelerators designed to reduce AWS dependency on Nvidia GPU pricing — was co-developed with Marvell as the silicon partner. Microsoft's Maia accelerator programme carried an equivalent relationship. The Google work went primarily to Broadcom. The programme-level scorecard, as reconstructed from public industry coverage, looked roughly as follows:

| Hyperscaler Programme | Principal Silicon Partner |
|---|---|
| Google TPU (v1–v6+) | Broadcom |
| Amazon Trainium | Marvell |
| Microsoft Maia | Marvell |
| Meta MTIA | Primarily internal |
| Apple neural engine | Internal |

Marvell's wins on Trainium and Maia gave it two of the four largest public cloud providers as active custom ASIC customers. The investor day framing from April 2024 presented a multi-billion-dollar custom silicon revenue opportunity across 2026 through 2028, grounded in the production ramp trajectories of these two programmes specifically, plus emerging engagements that remained unnamed at the time. Murphy described the custom silicon opportunity in that period as a demand environment "unlike anything we've observed in prior infrastructure cycles" — a characterisation that recurred across multiple earnings calls as the Trainium and Maia ramps moved from design to volume production.

The structural advantage Broadcom held was programme breadth and the singular depth of the Google relationship. The structural advantage Marvell held was timing and positioning: the Avera acquisition arrived precisely as Amazon and Microsoft were accelerating their custom silicon ambitions, and Marvell's design services capability was purpose-built for the multi-year co-development that Trainium and Maia required.

## Nvidia and AMD: Different Games

Against Nvidia, Marvell did not compete — at least not directly. The H100, H200, and successor Blackwell GPU architecture addressed a different buyer decision entirely: whether to purchase off-the-shelf accelerator compute rather than design it. Marvell's custom silicon thesis was explicitly predicated on the hyperscaler calculus shifting toward the latter, driven by total cost of ownership, workload specificity, and the strategic desire to reduce single-vendor exposure. In that framing, Nvidia's continued dominance in GPU merchant silicon was not a threat to Marvell so much as the condition that made Marvell's custom ASIC argument compelling — every dollar of Nvidia GPU revenue at elevated gross margins that a hyperscaler could replace with internally designed silicon at lower marginal cost was a dollar of motivation to fund a multi-year ASIC programme.

AMD's MI300X and MI400-series GPUs occupied the merchant accelerator tier below Nvidia. AMD competed with Nvidia; it did not compete with Marvell. The competitive dynamic between AMD and Nvidia had no direct bearing on Marvell's custom ASIC positioning, though it did influence the broader hyperscaler capital allocation environment. A world in which AMD successfully eroded some Nvidia GPU share was also a world in which hyperscalers had more negotiating leverage on merchant silicon — potentially accelerating their interest in custom alternatives precisely to avoid reconcentrating dependency on any single vendor.

## Electro-Optics: The Inphi Inheritance

If custom ASIC was Marvell's largest strategic bet, electro-optics was its most technically differentiated. The April 2021 acquisition of Inphi for approximately $10 billion brought a library of PAM-DSP and coherent DSP intellectual property that positioned Marvell at the core of the hyperscaler optical interconnect stack — the physical layer governing data movement between servers within and across data centre racks.

The competitive landscape in electro-optics operated at multiple layers. At the component and module level, Marvell faced Lumentum Holdings, which focused on laser and photonic components, and Coherent Corporation — the entity created by the 2022 merger of II-VI Incorporated and Coherent Corp — which offered an integrated transceiver portfolio spanning datacom and telecom applications. Chinese module makers including Innolight and Eoptolink competed at the 400G and 800G transceiver tier on price, increasingly challenging the Western supply chain economics at a time when hyperscalers were sensitive to cost per gigabit.

Marvell's competitive position in this landscape was specific: it competed at the DSP chip level, not the module level. The Inphi-derived PAM4 DSP — embedded in the 800G and 1.6T transceivers that hyperscalers were deploying in next-generation rack architectures — gave Marvell a position that was invisible in the finished module but central to signal fidelity at extreme throughput. Against Lumentum and Coherent in this DSP-layer competition, Marvell held the advantage of hyperscaler co-development relationships: the same Amazon and Microsoft engagements that drove custom AI silicon work also shaped the optical interconnect roadmap, because both problems — compute and interconnect — were being optimised simultaneously by the same infrastructure teams. Marvell's ability to present a unified silicon roadmap across compute and optics was a differentiation that neither Lumentum nor Coherent could replicate from their respective positions in the stack.

The 1.6T coherent optical interconnect reaching production qualification at hyperscalers through 2025 represented the next frontier of that franchise and the clearest expression of the Inphi thesis.

## Innovium and the Ethernet Switch Question

The October 2022 acquisition of Innovium for approximately $1.1 billion added a third competitive dimension: Ethernet switch silicon. Innovium's Teralynx architecture competed with Broadcom's Tomahawk family in the merchant switch silicon market — the segment determining switching capacity within hyperscaler data centres.

Broadcom's dominance in merchant Ethernet switching was, if anything, more entrenched than its custom ASIC position. The Tomahawk series had achieved a near-monopoly in hyperscaler switch silicon across multiple generations, and competitive displacement in this market was among the harder strategic tasks in semiconductors. Cisco's Silicon One programme offered an in-house alternative within Cisco's own networking equipment. Nvidia's Spectrum-X platform — inherited through the Mellanox acquisition — provided an RDMA-optimised switching option aimed specifically at AI cluster interconnect rather than general-purpose data centre fabrics.

Innovium's Teralynx positioned Marvell as a second-source option in merchant switch silicon, providing hyperscaler procurement teams an alternative to full Broadcom dependency across both compute and network. By the snapshot date the Teralynx franchise had not displaced Broadcom's Tomahawk at scale; the strategic value of Innovium was arguably as much a capability anchor — enabling Marvell to present a comprehensive silicon portfolio to infrastructure buyers — as an immediate revenue engine at competitive parity.

## The Durability Question

The central strategic question for Marvell, as the AI capex cycle moved from early ramp to sustained production through 2025 and 2026, was whether its two-programme custom ASIC franchise could expand against Broadcom's superior breadth and its own scale disadvantage.

The bull case rested on three pillars. First, Trainium and Maia were multi-generation programmes; design wins secured in 2023 and 2024 carried multi-year production tails that would sustain revenue regardless of near-term competitive pressure. Second, Marvell's integrated silicon roadmap — custom AI ASIC, optical DSP, and switch silicon under one roof — gave hyperscaler infrastructure teams a single counterparty for multiple cluster architecture components, a bundling advantage that neither pure-play optics vendors nor pure-play switching vendors could offer. Third, secular growth in hyperscaler AI capital expenditure, which multiple industry analysts estimated at compound double-digit rates through the late 2020s, implied that even a stable share of an expanding market would produce substantial absolute revenue growth — consistent with the Data Center segment's trajectory from 39 percent of total revenue in fiscal 2024 to approximately 50 percent in fiscal 2025 and approaching 70 percent by late fiscal 2026.

The bear case was structurally simpler: Broadcom was larger, held more programmes, controlled the Google relationship, and was accumulating additional AI-native customers. In a market where custom silicon programmes were won through decade-long engineering relationships and bleeding-edge process node expertise, Marvell's Avera-derived design capability, while genuine, remained a fraction of Broadcom's experienced ASIC workforce and its established co-packaging relationships with TSMC's advanced packaging operations.

What the competitive evidence through the snapshot date suggested was that the custom AI silicon market was large enough, and the hyperscaler demand signal strong enough, to sustain two principal merchant partners simultaneously — one anchored at Google with a growing AI-native franchise, one anchored at Amazon and Microsoft with strong optical DSP adjacency. The question was not whether Marvell could compete, but whether the hyperscaler demand trajectory would grow fast enough to validate the premium multiple at which Marvell shares traded and justify the $10 billion Inphi bet that had made the integrated thesis possible in the first place.

chapters.title: From 2018 Cavium through Inphi, AI custom silicon, and the September 2024 CFO transition
chapters.body:
## The Acquisition Arc as Catalyst Timeline

The four acquisitions detailed in the Snapshot — Cavium (2018), Avera (2019), Inphi (2021), Innovium (2022), totalling approximately $18 billion — each became visible as catalysts at different points in Marvell's stock narrative.

The Cavium integration was not seamless. Marvell absorbed a company with different engineering culture and product lines that did not immediately fit the company's gravitational centre. The Cavium bet was not a quick-turn trade — it was a platform acquisition whose value only became legible years later when custom-silicon opportunity became dominant.

Avera's $650 million price, modest relative to Cavium, proved one of the more efficient capability purchases in the AI buildout cycle. The acquisition provided both engineering methodology and contractual relationships that enabled the defining commercial bet of the Murphy era.

The Inphi timing — closing in April 2021, months before the first clear public signals of hyperscaler AI infrastructure acceleration — gave Marvell an optical-interconnect franchise exactly as data-centre architects were pricing in bandwidth demands of large-model training. The 1.6T co-packaged optics ramp sits at the direct intersection of AI cluster density and the physical-layer connectivity tax that limits it.

Innovium was the smallest acquisition and one with the most uncertain outcome at close. Displacing entrenched Broadcom switching relationships requires multi-year co-development cadence. Shah's organisation has positioned Teralynx as complement to custom-ASIC and electro-optics rather than standalone growth engine.

## The AI Custom Silicon Inflection

The commercial logic converged in calendar 2023–24 around the thesis that hyperscalers would design their own AI accelerators and need a partner with ASIC capability, process-node expertise, and packaging know-how. Marvell had assembled the only merchant franchise outside Broadcom capable of executing that role.

Bharathi's Custom Compute organisation runs Trainium and Maia at 3nm with 2nm engagements in the pipeline. The co-development model creates multi-year revenue relationships rather than transactional merchant-silicon dynamics.

## The April 2024 Investor Day

The investor day served as the clearest public articulation of the custom-silicon growth thesis — framing addressable revenue in the multi-billion-dollar range across FY2026–28. Murphy framed the opportunity as generational:

> "The amount of capital that these large cloud providers are spending on AI infrastructure is unlike anything we've ever seen in the semiconductor industry. And Marvell is right in the middle of it."

The event also provided first detailed public discussion of the 1.6T optical interconnect roadmap — the principal forward catalyst cited by sell-side analysts.

## The CFO Transition

The September 2024 CFO transition from Hu to Meintjes came as the finance function's principal challenge shifted from integration accounting to programme revenue forecasting at AI-infrastructure scale. Hu had overseen Inphi and Innovium integrations and the FY2024 revenue compression period.

The acquisition arc produced a Data Center franchise positioning Marvell as principal merchant infrastructure partner to hyperscalers outside the Nvidia-Broadcom dyad. Whether the multi-billion-dollar projections Murphy set out in April 2024 are realised is the central question the post-Meintjes CFO regime will have to answer.

chapters.title: Custom ASIC IP, PAM-DSP optics, Ethernet switch silicon, and the 5nm/3nm/2nm roadmap
chapters.body:
## The IP Mosaic

Marvell's technology advantage rests on a calculated accumulation of engineering capabilities. The three technology-driven acquisitions (Avera, Inphi, Innovium) each deposited a distinct IP layer: coherent DSP patents from Inphi, custom-silicon design methodology from Avera's IBM lineage, and merchant Ethernet switch IP from Innovium — a stack covering the signal-processing backbone of a modern AI hyperscaler pod from chip to optical fibre.

## Custom-ASIC Design Engine

Avera brought roughly 700 experienced engineers with deep expertise in RTL design, physical implementation on advanced nodes, and the long-cycle engagement model hyperscalers demand. The custom-ASIC model is not simple manufacturing pass-through: Marvell contributes proprietary silicon IP — interface blocks, memory controllers, interconnect fabric — into the customer's chip architecture, making it a genuine design co-author.

Murphy described the structural advantage: Marvell's ability to bring proven, silicon-validated IP blocks shortens the path from architecture to tape-out by a material margin. Each successful programme generates additional IP recyclable into subsequent engagements, compounding the portfolio's depth.

## PAM-DSP and the Optical Interconnect Stack

Inphi's COLORZ coherent DSP line had established deep hyperscaler relationships. Post-acquisition, Marvell extended the PAM-DSP architecture toward 800G and 1.6T line rates. The 1.6T DSP chipsets represent the most demanding signal-processing integration shipped: managing nonlinear distortion, chromatic dispersion, and polarisation-mode dispersion simultaneously across tens of kilometres.

[Light Counting](https://www.lightcounting.com) tracked the migration from 400G to 800G as the dominant standard through 2024–25, with 1.6T programmes beginning qualification. Because each GPU cluster generation requires higher-radix optical interconnect, demand scales in rough proportion to AI capex — a structural linkage distinguishing Marvell's franchise from commodity module assembly.

The patent estate reinforces the competitive moat: thousands of active grants covering Ethernet physical-layer technology, coherent DSP algorithms, high-speed SerDes, and custom-ASIC methodology.

## Teralynx Switch Silicon

The Teralynx family — competitive with Broadcom Tomahawk at 12.8Tbps fabric throughput — was engineered for leaf-spine fabrics where port density, power efficiency, and programmability are primary competitive variables. The underlying IP includes a programmable pipeline architecture allowing custom forwarding behaviours without sacrificing throughput — resonant in hyperscaler environments with increasingly proprietary software stacks.

## Process Node Roadmap: 5nm, 3nm, and 2nm

Marvell's migration to TSMC's five-nanometre node represented commitment to leading-edge silicon as competitive differentiator. The AI custom silicon programmes use N5/N4 derivatives; transistor density and performance-per-watt are essential for power-constrained accelerator trays.

The three-nanometre generation (N3) entered the pipeline for next-generation custom AI silicon and optical DSPs. N5-to-N3 delivers meaningful die-area reduction, translating to smaller chips or more functionality per reticle limit — essential to keep power practical as accelerator complexity grows.

The two-nanometre node (N2, nanosheet gate-all-around architecture) appeared on Marvell's forward agenda. CoWoS advanced packaging — integrating multiple chiplets on a silicon interposer — is a complementary investment. Custom AI silicon engagements increasingly depend on CoWoS capacity allocation, placing Marvell in direct competition with other leading-edge fabless companies.

## R&D Investment and Portfolio Depth

R&D expenditure approximated one-third of FY2025 revenue — reflecting ongoing integration of acquired IP and the front-loaded cost structure where NRE spending precedes revenue recognition by years.

That intensity is the price of maintaining position at the leading edge of three converging curves: AI accelerator silicon, high-speed optical DSP, and merchant switch fabric. It is also, from an investor perspective, an option on future custom-silicon programmes — each engagement requires validated IP libraries, experienced teams, and successful tape-out track record.

chapters.title: Custom silicon programme concentration, Broadcom competitive intensity, AI cycle, China exposure
chapters.body:
Marvell's transformation into an AI infrastructure company has brought rewards commensurate with the structural risks embedded in that repositioning. Six categorical vulnerabilities define the bear case: concentration within two dominant custom-silicon programmes, the shadow of Broadcom's scale and incumbent relationships, the cyclicality inherent in any capex-driven technology expansion, the continuing drag of China export restrictions, a single-foundry dependence on TSMC, and the indirect but material constraint of high-bandwidth memory supply. Together, they form the lens through which a risk-adjusted assessment of Marvell's forward earnings power must be made.

## Custom silicon programme concentration

The most immediate structural concern is concentration in two relationships: Trainium and Maia. Both represent years of co-development embedded in multi-node design cycles. That intimacy creates concentration exposure that, were either programme to stall or be brought partially in-house, would register visibly in revenue trajectory.

With Data Center approaching 70 percent of revenue by FY2026 Q4, and within that segment dependency on Amazon and Microsoft above all others, the programme-level risk was not theoretical.

The mitigants were genuine. Design cycles span three to five years — next-generation derivatives were already embedded in cost base before reaching production. Switching suppliers mid-programme would require re-tapeout at tens of millions per iteration; the switching cost is multi-year roadmap delay, not financial penalty. Google provided an additional anchor.

The concern was that Amazon and Microsoft retained full strategic discretion. Both maintained internal teams capable of expanding in-house scope — Amazon through Annapurna Labs, Microsoft through its silicon organisation. Partial insourcing could compress programme economics over successive generations.

## Broadcom competitive intensity

Marvell occupied second chair in merchant custom-ASIC — genuine commercial strength, but defined partly by what it was not. Broadcom held the Google TPU programme, conferring scale advantages in engineering capacity and hyperscaler credibility. Broadcom's AI revenue grew substantially faster than the broader market through 2023–25.

The competitive asymmetry was real. Broadcom's consolidated revenue exceeded $50 billion (FY October 2024), providing cost structure and development budget Marvell could not match. Tomahawk retained dominant share in hyperscaler spine switching; displacing an incumbent with decade-long relationships was a multi-generation proposition.

Marvell's countervailing strengths lay in specificity: the optical DSP franchise occupied a lane where Broadcom's depth was thinner, and the Avera-heritage design methodology offered IBM-era process discipline Broadcom's more product-centric organisation did not replicate. Whether differentiation would sustain as Broadcom intensified custom silicon investment was among the more consequential open questions.

## AI cycle moderation

The bull case for Marvell rested on a sustained, multi-year ramp in hyperscaler AI capital expenditure—an assumption that had been directionally correct through early 2026 but which carried meaningful mean-reversion risk. Capital expenditure cycles in technology infrastructure have not historically been linear. The period from 2022 through early 2026 was characterised by extraordinary front-loading of AI training infrastructure as hyperscalers competed to build foundational model capacity; a period of digestion, in which clusters were utilised rather than expanded, would directly pressure Marvell's custom silicon shipment volumes.

The non-Data Center segments provided little cyclical buffer. Carrier infrastructure and enterprise networking remained compressed through most of the 2023–2025 period, and automotive and industrial remained subscale contributors to consolidated revenue. If the AI spending cycle moderated before those segments recovered, Marvell's revenue mix would offer limited defensive depth.

The structural mitigant was the shift toward AI inference at scale. Inference—the deployment of trained models against production query loads—created a demand profile more predictable and more durable than training, which was episodic and tied to the cadence of frontier model releases. As hyperscalers expanded inference infrastructure, demand for custom accelerators was likely to become more evenly distributed across the calendar than concentrated in capacity-build phases. Murphy had consistently emphasised this dynamic in earnings commentary, framing inference expansion as a second, overlapping growth vector atop the training infrastructure buildout.

## China exposure and export controls

Marvell's China exposure was more limited than peers with significant consumer or telecom component businesses, but it was not immaterial. Export controls introduced by the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security from October 2022 onward progressively restricted the sale of advanced semiconductors to Chinese counterparties. For Marvell, the principal channel of historical exposure had been Chinese carrier and enterprise customers purchasing networking and storage components; the hyperscaler custom silicon programmes were U.S.-domiciled and therefore outside the control regime.

The risk operated at two levels. Direct revenue from Chinese customers contracted as restrictions tightened through the 2023–2025 cycle. Any further escalation—whether through Entity List additions, expanded Foreign Direct Product Rule coverage, or broader technology decoupling—would narrow Marvell's addressable market in the world's largest semiconductor consumption geography. Indirectly, the decoupling dynamic accelerated Chinese domestic investment in semiconductor design and manufacturing; over a medium-term horizon, that substitution could reduce Chinese demand for merchant silicon from U.S. suppliers even in segments not currently restricted.

| Segment | China exposure | Export control sensitivity |
|---|---|---|
| Custom AI silicon | Minimal (U.S. hyperscaler programmes) | Low |
| Electro-optics / DSP | Moderate (carrier deployments) | Medium-high |
| Enterprise networking | Moderate | Medium |
| Carrier infrastructure | Elevated | High |

## Foundry dependence on TSMC

Marvell was a fabless company. Its advanced-node products—including the custom AI silicon co-developed with Amazon and Microsoft—were manufactured at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. That dependence was shared across the fabless industry but concentrated geopolitical and capacity-allocation risk in a single supplier operating principally from Taiwan.

A sustained disruption to TSMC's advanced-node capacity—whether from a Taiwan Strait military contingency, a natural disaster, or a regulatory restriction—had no near-term substitute. Intel Foundry Services and Samsung Foundry had each pursued advanced-node customers, but neither had demonstrated yield and volume capacity at N3 and N2 comparable to TSMC through the period under review. TSMC's Arizona facility expansion would eventually provide geographic diversification, but volumes through U.S. fabs remained a fraction of total advanced-node capacity as of early 2026.

Capacity allocation was a subtler but more proximate risk. As AI silicon demand concentrated among a handful of large fabless customers—Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Broadcom, Marvell—priority access at TSMC's most advanced nodes had become a competitive variable. A Marvell programme de-prioritised in a tight allocation environment would miss product ramp timing, potentially handing competitors a window to deepen hyperscaler relationships during Marvell's gap.

## HBM supply constraints

High-bandwidth memory was not manufactured by Marvell, but it was integral to the custom AI accelerators Marvell designed. Trainium and Maia, like nearly all large AI training chips, relied on HBM stacked adjacent to or atop the logic die to sustain the memory bandwidth demanded by transformer-architecture workloads. Supply of HBM—concentrated among SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron—had periodically constrained system-level deployment even when logic silicon was available.

The constraint operated as an indirect revenue ceiling. If Amazon or Microsoft could not procure sufficient HBM to populate custom accelerator deployments at the planned rate, shipments of Marvell-designed logic chips were deferred regardless of Marvell's own production status. HBM supply expanded through 2024 and 2025 as all three DRAM manufacturers prioritised the product line, but demand growth from Nvidia, the custom ASIC ecosystem, and emerging accelerator entrants absorbed capacity gains in roughly equal measure. Near-term supply-demand balance in HBM remained a swing factor in AI infrastructure deployment timing and, therefore, an indirect variable in Marvell's revenue cadence that management could neither control nor fully hedge.

Taken together, these six risks described a company operating at the intersection of durable secular tailwinds and concentrated structural dependencies. The AI infrastructure thesis remained intact through the frozen window; the question a risk-adjusted investor was required to hold alongside that thesis was which dependency, at what programme cycle or geopolitical inflection, would constrain rather than enable the next phase of the franchise.

chapters.title: Custom silicon scaling, 1.6T optics, and the FY2027-FY2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## Custom silicon at scale: the FY2027 ramp enters its steepest phase

By FY2026 Q4, the custom AI silicon programmes were the company's dominant revenue engine, with Data Center approaching 70 percent of total revenue. The question entering FY2027 was not whether the franchise had arrived, but whether it could sustain velocity across a four-year corridor testing every assumption about hyperscaler capex durability, competitive moat depth, and execution bandwidth.

The FY2027–30 case rests on three pillars: second- and third-generation custom AI silicon at a broadening roster of hyperscalers; 1.6T optical interconnect adoption; and eventual recovery of carrier/enterprise segments.

## Custom AI silicon: from programme launches to volume production

Trainium2 had entered AWS UltraServer infrastructure at scale. Marvell's contribution extended beyond core silicon to include high-speed SerDes IP and packaging integration — differentiation AWS could not easily source elsewhere. Maia represented Microsoft's strategic commitment to reduce Nvidia H100/Blackwell dependence.

The April 2024 analyst day trajectory appeared to be tracking ahead of original modelling by the snapshot date, driven by faster-than-anticipated hyperscaler capex and programme base broadening. Google's custom silicon engagement represented a potential third major volume ramp in FY2027–28.

| Programme | Customer | Status (May 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| Trainium2 | AWS | Production ramp |
| Maia | Azure | Production ramp |
| TPU-adjacent | Google | In development |

Broadcom retained dominance through Alphabet, but Marvell had demonstrated it could manage tier-one hyperscaler programme complexity — a credential creating defensible differentiation where programme history weighs heavily in vendor selection.

## 1.6T optics: from qualification to volume inflection

The electro-optics franchise had navigated two generational transitions (100G→400G, 400G→800G) before 1.6T. Each transition concentrated the market around fewer suppliers; Marvell's position strengthened at each prior node.

The 1.6T transition carries structurally larger economics: ASPs increase, integration complexity favours established suppliers, and 18–24 month qualification cycles create meaningful barriers. Marvell's Orion DSP platform had entered qualification at multiple hyperscalers by mid-FY2026. Primary optical research projects the 1.6T market reaching multiple billions by 2027–28.

The demand backdrop supports timing: cluster sizes expanding from thousands to tens of thousands of accelerators imply non-linear interconnect bandwidth scaling. At those scales, optical is structural necessity, not incremental upgrade.

## Switch silicon and non-Data Center recovery

By FY2026, Ethernet fabric adoption for AI training clusters — driven by preference for open-standard alternatives to InfiniBand — created favourable Teralynx demand. Marvell's ability to bundle switch, custom accelerator, and optical DSPs represents a cross-sell dynamic unavailable to pure-play vendors.

Carrier/enterprise/consumer segments endured prolonged FY2024–25 compression. FY2027–28 represents credible recovery corridor — lower execution risk and more predictable cash generation, a relevant stabiliser amid custom programme ramp volatility.

## Risks to the FY2030 horizon

Programme concentration remains the most structurally significant risk — two or three engagements dominate the custom silicon trajectory. Reprioritisation of Trainium or Maia would create revenue gaps difficult to replace within a fiscal year.

Co-packaged optics threatens to alter the supply chain in ways that might disadvantage standalone DSP suppliers over FY2028–30. Marvell has been developing CPO capability, but commercial timeline and competitive dynamics remain unresolved.

Execution risk — schedule slippage, yield issues, performance shortfalls — remains a permanent model feature. Hyperscaler capex sensitivity to macro conditions (visible during 2022–23 digestion) is a reminder that AI infrastructure investment is not structurally immune to external pressures.

## The durability question

Marvell's central claim is that it assembled the only integrated custom silicon and hyperscaler optics franchise outside the Nvidia-Broadcom duopoly. The honest qualification: durability will be measured by whether Marvell secures third and fourth generation hyperscaler engagements — programmes whose specifications do not yet exist on any public roadmap. Incumbency helps but does not guarantee continuity. The next four years will determine whether evidence accumulates faster than risks materialise.
